I've seen some criticisms of Lean4 regarding the size and complexity of both its kernel & runtime after the recent 0-day discovered in the runtime: https://x.com/kirancodes/status/2043735565640585656

Are there any efforts to reduce Lean4's TCB? If so, how can I get involved? If not, why not? I'm interested in leveraging Lean4 to do some program verification of compiler & language tooling but these takes have made me a bit more skeptical.

More context on associated discussion: https://x.com/JustDeezGuy/status/2043757783703503269?s=20

Interesting, maybe I missed it and this is a silly question, but was a specific theorem in lean-zip identified as type checked by the kernel that is actually false, proven with the buffer overflow? It is certainly a bug, I am just not sure how it would could break a proof that is in Prop, but I am not at all an expert in the programming side, so am interested to learn. Is the claim it is the theorem zlib_decompressSingle_compress?
If I understand correctly, the proof is sound, but the compiled executable doesn't behave as it's supposed to due to a bug.

I don't think anything discussed there touches on the kernel.

src/kernel has ~8k of code, there are multiple independent implementations (see arena.lean-lang.org), and a manual on implementing it (https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/title_page.html) so it is a nontrivial but reasonable task to audit it yourself.

Program verification is a big lift and there is a lot of interesting work ongoing in this direction.
Has anyone got a better link than "random twitter post claims bug"? I didn't see a discussion in #lean4 for example. I am by default skeptical of this claim until I see more evidence.
There is no kernel bug. There is a bug in the runtime, namely lean4#13388.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Has anyone got a better link than "random twitter post claims bug"? I didn't see a discussion in #lean4 for example. I am by default skeptical of this claim until I see more evidence.

As author of random twitter post, and article, there waa a bug, patched shortly after publishing the article. (The github issue was linked in the article fwiw)

Its not relevant to mathematicians I suppose, but for formal verification purposes it is salient. If one verifies a system in lean, one would hope it is free of memory exploits. The domains where formal verification is critical (e.g. airplane software, embedded systems etc.) do care a lot about such issues.

The fact that there was one in the runtime is relevant to anyone who wants to use lean for formal verification, of which there is increasing interest.

There are two TCBs that we have to talk about here:

  1. The kernel itself which is the TCB for when it comes to accepting proofs, this is the TCB that is important for mathematicians and theorists of any kind when it comes to using Lean. Finding an issue in this one would allow you to do a proof of False. In an adversarial scenario you should additionally also use comparator to check the proof. The code affected by this issue is not called in comparator (or the kernel) at all so this does not enable a proof of False. As for Paul Snively's comment, as others have brought up the TCB for this is merely 8k LoC and there do even exist multiple implementations of the kernel that you can use interchangably. Paul goes on to claim that the kernel isn't amenable to human audit and also that Rocq's kernel is only 500 lines of code. Both of these are wrong. Of course a human can read the 8k lines of code (and several have done so) and Rocq's kernel is approximately 18k LoC as the Rocq developers say themselves.
  2. When you are executing Lean code compiled by our compiler you of course trust that the compiler preserves the semantics of the program and that our runtime is correct. The bug found by this fuzzing campaign requires an attacker to control the size of an array allocation you are about to make in a running Lean program (and then some luck and additional difficulties) to get somewhere. Common ways to get around this "gap" would be to verify the Lean runtime and compiler itself (which is not planned any time soon though), to verify code written in e.g. C or Rust (potentially generated using a DSL from Lean) with tooling like Aeneas, or to reason on the binary directly like seL4 or several projects at AWS do. As for the claim that our runtime is ~100k LoC of C++, even if you count all of the C++ including the kernel (which is not usually part of the executable) they sum up to approximately 32k LoC of C++. I would assume that the count from the tweet was done including the stage0/ directory which contains the compiler that we use for bootstrapping Lean so not really part of the TCB when executing Lean code.
Thanks for the summary, it’s good to get the facts straight. I hope these clarifications diffuse from here to the other platforms :-)

Appreciate the detailed response @Henrik Böving. Good to clarify the misconceptions.

Based on the response then it seems like the best way to rely on Lean4 verification is via proofs checked by the kernel vs. as an example a verified Lean verifier/reproducer function compiled to a linkable library / program you call out to?

Also if my proof relies on evaluation or folding of Lean4 functions does that hinge solely on the kernel or the runtime, do things like decide every rely on the runtime to fill in the gaps?

Also if my proof relies on evaluation or folding of Lean4 functions does that hinge solely on the kernel or the runtime, do things like decide every rely on the runtime to fill in the gaps?

No, the runtime is not involved in any sort of unfold, decide, cbv_decide proof. The tool that requires trusting the runtime would be proofs by native_decide (or tools building on native_decide such as bv_decide). However, the individual statements proven by native_decide are injected as axioms into the Lean environment so they are auditable, for example:

def test : Nat := 1

theorem foo : test + test = 2 := by native_decide

#print axioms foo -- 'foo' depends on axioms: [foo._native.native_decide.ax_1_1]
#check foo._native.native_decide.ax_1_1 -- foo._native.native_decide.ax_1_1 : decide (test + test = 2) = true

Thus actually checking a proof in the Lean kernel does not execute code in the Lean runtime (so in particular third party kernels can have truly disjoint code bases from the default kernel in principle)
Not just in principle; the Rust-implemented nanoda checker has a truly disjoint code base.

Just for fun, I vibe coded the kernel in solidity(ethereum smart contract). Frankly not sure where I am going with this that but sounded like a fun idea to implement and have another checker. https://github.com/FawadHa1der/evm_proof_checker. Would love to work on this further and have it included in the Lean kernel arena. Any tips on that ?
Are you able to run it as a local CLI tool somehow? Then you can create a PR against the arena to add it as a checker there.

yep HOWTO-ARENA.md has instructions how to download the arena tests and run against it. It has 75 tests apart from that as well.
Once you have downloaded the arena tests you do this

node tools/run-arena-tests.js /tmp/lean-arena-tests --tutorial

node tools/run-arena-tests.js /tmp/lean-arena-tests --entrypoint-max-bytes=128000 --allow-non-tutorial-decline

There is a limit on transaction size for ethereum and that's why it can't test 4 big tests but all else seem to be working. I am sure there are some gaps since this vibe coded but still interesting that it can be done.
Sounds good! If you plan to maintain it and keep it alive, it's welcome on the arena
